title: Matplotlib Logic
blurb: Run the plotting code in your head: subplot grids, the artists that calls return, and who pyplot's commands really act on.

cells.title: A figure is a container of axes
cells.body:
Every matplotlib drawing lives inside a two-level hierarchy: the Figure is the whole canvas — the thing you save or show — and each Axes is one plot area with its own x-axis, y-axis, title and artists. When you call plt.subplots(nrows, ncols) you get back the figure plus an array of axes shaped (nrows, ncols) — the same order you passed in.

The indexing habit to build: axes[row, col], where row 0 is the TOP row — like a table, not like data coordinates. The figure also keeps a flat list, fig.axes, in creation order (row-major), so the last axes created is the bottom-right one. Knowing both views of the same objects lets you simulate indexing questions without running anything.

demo.code:
nrows, ncols = 2, 3
axes = [['ax[%d,%d]' % (r, c) for c in range(ncols)] for r in range(nrows)]
print('shape:', (len(axes), len(axes[0])))
for row in axes:
    print(row)
print('top-right subplot    -> axes[0, 2] =', axes[0][2])
print('bottom-left subplot  -> axes[1, 0] =', axes[1][0])

cells.title: Plot calls return artists
cells.body:
Matplotlib calls are not fire-and-forget: every plotting method returns the artists it created. ax.plot(x, y) returns a list of Line2D objects — one per series in the call — and the axes also keeps them in ax.lines. That is why lines = ax.plot(x, y) lets you later call lines[0].set_color('red') to restyle one specific series.

Two habits follow. First, the return value is always a list, even for a single series, so you can unpack it uniformly. Second, a multi-series call like ax.plot(x, y1, 'o-', x, y2, 's--') creates one artist per (x, y, fmt) group — the format string 's--' means marker 's' plus linestyle '--'. Counting artists correctly is the first step to animating or restyling exactly the series you meant to touch.

demo.code:
class FakeAxes:
    def __init__(self):
        self.lines = []
    def plot(self, *groups):
        made = ['Line2D#%d' % (len(self.lines) + i + 1)
                for i in range(len(groups))]
        self.lines.extend(made)
        return made

ax = FakeAxes()
result = ax.plot(('x', 'y1'), ('x', 'y2'))
print('plot() returned:', result)
print('same objects the axes keeps:', result[0] is ax.lines[0])
print('ax.lines now holds:', len(ax.lines), 'artists')

cells.title: Two interfaces and one hidden pointer
cells.body:
Pyplot is a state machine: commands like plt.plot(...) and plt.title(...) do not name their target — they act on the current figure and, inside it, the current axes: the most recently created ones. The object-oriented interface (ax.set_title(...), fig.savefig(...)) names its target explicitly, which is why it is the recommended style for scripts and functions.

The classic surprise: after fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2), the current axes is ax2 — the last one created — so the next plt.plot(...) draws on the right panel, not the left. And ax.twinx() stacks a second axes on top of ax sharing its x-axis (with a new y-axis drawn on the right) — and that new twin becomes the current axes too. When you can predict where a pyplot call will land, mixing the two interfaces stops being dangerous.

exercise.title: Predict: the subplot grid
exercise.statement: No coding here — run the snippet in your head. You are building a dashboard and need to know exactly what plt.subplots(2, 3) hands you before writing any indexing code. Predict what this prints (the two is checks compare against the figure's flat list of axes, fig.axes).
exercise.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3)
print(axes.shape)
print(axes[1, 2] is fig.axes[-1])
print(axes[0, 2] is fig.axes[2])
exercise.explain: subplots(nrows, ncols) returns an axes array shaped exactly like the arguments you passed: (2, 3). Axes are created row-major (all of row 0 first), and row 0 is the TOP row — so axes[0, 2] is the top-right subplot, created third, which makes it fig.axes[2]. The last axes created is the bottom-right one, axes[1, 2], so axes[1, 2] is fig.axes[-1] is True. fig.axes holds the very same objects — never copies — so both identity checks pass. B swaps the shape to (cols, rows); C assumes fig.axes stores copies of the axes; D forgets that the array only flattens when one dimension is 1 — subplots(1, 6) would return a 1-D array, but subplots(2, 3) is genuinely 2-D.

exercise.title: Predict: what plot() hands back
exercise.statement: Reading library code in your head again — this time about return values. A colleague restyles charts by grabbing whatever ax.plot returns, and you are reviewing their indexing before the code runs. Predict what this prints.
exercise.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
x = [0, 1, 2]
out = ax.plot(x, [1, 2, 4], 'o-',
              x, [1, 4, 9], 's--')
print(type(out).__name__, len(out))
print(out[0].get_marker(), out[1].get_marker(), out[1].get_linestyle())
print(len(ax.lines))
exercise.explain: Each (x, y, fmt) group inside one plot call becomes its own Line2D artist, and the method returns them as a list: two groups here, so list 2. The format string 's--' splits into marker 's' and linestyle '--', while 'o-' gives marker 'o' with linestyle '-' — printed as o s --. The axes registers every line in ax.lines, so it holds 2 artists. A is the single-artist belief — even a one-series call returns a 1-element list, which is exactly why out[0] always works; B has the right count but the wrong container type (a list, not a tuple); D is right until the last line — ax.lines counts artists, not plot() calls.

exercise.title: Predict: pyplot vs the object interface
exercise.statement: Time to predict the picture, not just printed text. This snippet mixes the pyplot interface with the object-oriented one, then adds a twin axis. Without running it, decide which figure you would see if plt.show() ran at the end.
exercise.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = [0, 1, 2, 3]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, [1, 2, 4, 8], color='tab:blue')
ax.set_ylabel('sensor reading')    # OO: explicitly on ax
plt.title('state machine')         # pyplot: on the CURRENT axes
ax.set_title('OO wins')            # OO: replaces the title on ax

ax2 = ax.twinx()                   # twin axes: shares x, new y on the right
ax2.plot(x, [8, 4, 2, 1], color='tab:red')
options: A. One plot area, blue line on the left y-axis, red line on the right y-axis, shared x — and the title at the top reads 'state machine'.
B. One plot area, blue line on the left y-axis, red line on the right y-axis, shared x — and the title at the top reads 'OO wins'.
C. Two side-by-side panels: the blue line in the left panel, the red line in the right panel, each panel with its own y-axis.
D. A RuntimeError at ax.set_title: an axes can only receive its title through one of the two interfaces.
exercise.explain: plt.title('state machine') routes to plt.gca() — the current axes. At that moment ax is the only (and most recently created) axes, so the title lands on ax. Then ax.set_title('OO wins') replaces that text: a title is a single Text artist, and the later call wins, so the figure shows 'OO wins'. twinx() does not split the figure (that would be subplots(1, 2)); it stacks a second axes at the same position, sharing the x-axis, with its own y-axis drawn on the right — so both curves appear in one plot area. D is backwards: the two interfaces are two doors to the same object — plt.title is literally implemented as gca().set_title, and calling both is perfectly legal; the last call simply overwrites. One extra trap to remember: after ax.twinx(), the twin becomes the current axes, so a later plt.* call would hit ax2 — one more reason the explicit OO style is safer in scripts.

exercise.title: Predict: cla, clf and close
exercise.statement: The deepest prediction challenge in this notebook: figure lifecycle. The script saves four PNGs while clearing and closing things along the way. Predict what b.png and c.png contain, and what happens on the final savefig call.
exercise.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
ax.set_title('run 1')
plt.savefig('a.png')      # chart with the line + title

ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 1])
plt.cla()                 # clear current axes
plt.savefig('b.png')

plt.clf()                 # clear current figure
plt.savefig('c.png')

plt.close(fig)            # destroy the figure
plt.savefig('d.png')      # ...and now?
options: A. b.png keeps only the second line (cla clears everything plotted before it); c.png is an empty axes frame; d.png is a copy of c.png.
B. b.png is a fully blank canvas with no axes; c.png is an empty axes frame — the two clearing calls have swapped effects.
C. The final plt.savefig('d.png') raises a RuntimeError: the figure it should save was closed, so no file is written.

D. b.png is an empty axes frame (both lines and the title gone, the axes box remains); c.png is a fully blank canvas; d.png is written without error — pyplot silently creates a fresh empty figure and saves that.
exercise.explain: Three calls, three scopes. plt.cla() = clear axes: it removes every artist on the current axes — both lines and the title, because a title is just a Text artist — but the axes object stays in the figure, so b.png shows an empty frame. plt.clf() = clear figure: it removes every axes from the figure, which itself survives as an empty canvas, so c.png is pure background. plt.close(fig) unregisters and destroys the figure; but plt.savefig always works on gcf() ('get current figure'), and gcf() lazily creates a brand-new figure when none is open — so d.png is saved as a blank canvas with no exception at all, a silent surprise. A invents a 'clear-only-older-artists' rule; B swaps cla and clf; C overestimates pyplot's strictness — the annoying truth is that it fails silently.
